ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was provided by the Department of Psychology Ethics Committee at the
table.header: PRE-REGISTERED HYPOTHESES

table.text: Participants are asked to respond to the position of the stimulus as quickly as possible by pressing a corresponding key on the keyboard.
table.header: INTRODUCTION

table.text: Additionally, (Lum et al., 2013) observed that the size of the difference between groups diminished with age when participants had more practice on the SRTT or when they were tested on a SRTT with a second order conditional sequence (i.e. higher order sequences involve the determination of which stimulus (n) will follow is based on element n-2).
table.formatted: Additionally, <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Lum et al., 2013)</ref> observed that the size of the difference between groups diminished with age when participants had more practice on the SRTT or when they were tested on a SRTT with a second order conditional sequence (i.e. higher order sequences involve the determination of which stimulus (n) will follow is based on element n-2).
table.header: INTRODUCTION

table.text: Participants are expected to demonstrate evidence of procedural learning in all sessions.
table.header: PRE-REGISTERED HYPOTHESES

table.text: All participants were native English speakers, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision.
table.header: PRE-REGISTERED HYPOTHESES

table.text: Participants were recruited through various avenues, including Prolific, the participant panel at the Department of Psychology, University of York, and social media, and were compensated with £15 or a £15 Amazon gift voucher for their time.
table.header: PRE-REGISTERED HYPOTHESES

table.text: Participants were presented with an array of four rectangles displayed horizontally, with a stimulus (smiley face) appearing in one of the four positions on each trial.
table.header: DESIGN AND MATERIALS

table.text: Participants are asked to press the corresponding key on the keyboard to the position of the stimulus on screen as soon as possible.
table.header: DESIGN AND MATERIALS

table.text: The SRTT comprised two second order conditional 12 items sequences for each session, the pairs of sequences were randomised across participants, resulting in six groups, and were taken from (Shanks et al., 2003) httpshttpshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qlieGv//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?h0TIsi//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wmpWEe probable sequence A -314324213412; improbable sequence B -431241321423; (Schvaneveldt & Gomez, 1998) : probable sequence C -121342314324; improbable sequence D -123413214243; and (Kaufman et al., 2010) : probable sequence E -121432413423; improbable sequence F -323412431421.
table.formatted: The SRTT comprised two second order conditional 12 items sequences for each session, the pairs of sequences were randomised across participants, resulting in six groups, and were taken from <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Shanks et al., 2003)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wmpWEe">:</ref> probable sequence A -314324213412; improbable sequence B -431241321423; <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Schvaneveldt & Gomez, 1998)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?h0TIsi">:</ref> probable sequence C -121342314324; improbable sequence D -123413214243; and <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Kaufman et al., 2010)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qlieGv">:</ref> probable sequence E -121432413423; improbable sequence F -323412431421.
table.header: DESIGN AND MATERIALS

table.text: The first generation task, under inclusion conditions, required each participant to generate 100 guesses of the sequence learned in the SRT task in the last session; whilst in the exclusion condition participants were asked to produce a sequence as different as possible from the training sequence.
table.header: DESIGN AND MATERIALS

table.text: Following the generation tasks, the attention abilities of the participants were assessed using a self-report questionnaire -Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS) whilst nonverbal intelligence was assessed through the Reasoning Matrix task from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence -II (WASI-II).
table.header: DESIGN AND MATERIALS

table.text: Random slopes for each participant/session were obtained by running a linear mixed effects model with response time as a dependent variable and probability and group as predictors, for the random structure participants were introduced as a random intercept and probability as a slope.
table.header: H2: Assessing the reliability of the procedural learning effect

table.text: Data from 17 participants (dyslexia: N = 7; TD: N = 10) was removed from the analyses as these did not meet inclusion criteria (i.e. dyslexic participants performing above the 90 percentile on at least one of the literacy measures and controls performing below the 90th percentile on literacy measures).
table.header: RESULTS

table.text: Since in the exclusion condition, unlike the inclusion condition, participants are asked to not generate the underlying sequence, this suggests some evidence of control over the explicit knowledge.
table.header: H5: Assessing group differences in explicit awareness

table.text: This is especially relevant when participants are being tested in a naturalistic setting where distractors are more likely to occur.
table.header: DISCUSSION

table.text: Secondly, if dyslexic participants are indeed able to fully compensate for their procedural learning deficits on the SRTT, it is unclear why the dyslexic group included in this study has not been able to compensate as well with the declarative system for their literacy and phonological abilities.
table.header: DISCUSSION

> Random slopes for each participant/session were obtained by running a linear mixed effects model with response time as a dependent variable and probability and group as predictors, for the random structure participants were introduced as a random intercept and probability as a slope.

> Data from 17 participants (dyslexia: N = 7; TD: N = 10) was removed from the analyses as these did not meet inclusion criteria (i.e. dyslexic participants performing above the 90 percentile on at least one of the literacy measures and controls performing below the 90th percentile on literacy measures).

> Since in the exclusion condition, unlike the inclusion condition, participants are asked to not generate the underlying sequence, this suggests some evidence of control over the explicit knowledge.

> This is especially relevant when participants are being tested in a naturalistic setting where distractors are more likely to occur.

> Secondly, if dyslexic participants are indeed able to fully compensate for their procedural learning deficits on the SRTT, it is unclear why the dyslexic group included in this study has not been able to compensate as well with the declarative system for their literacy and phonological abilities.

table.title: Does attentional difficulties place adults with dyslexia at a higher risk for procedural learning deficits?
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
The experiment uses a mixed-subjects design with each participant performing the Serial Reaction Time task at three time points each separated by roughly one week. The three underlying sequences of the SRT task will be counterbalanced to avoid order effects. Participants will be allocated to one of two groups: (i) TD adults and (ii) Dyslexia group based on diagnosis criteria and performance on the literacy tasks.
A battery of tests will be administered after the SRT task in all sessions. In the first session, literacy abilities (reading and spelling tasks and reading questionnaire) will be assessed, whilst the language (nonword repetition, sentence repetition and vocabulary) measures will be tested in session 2 and in session 3 the Conners questionnaire, nonverbal intelligence and explicit awareness tasks will be administered. At the end of each session, sustained attention will be measured using an adapted version of the Psychomotor Vigilance task (Reifman et al., 2018) to explore the relationship between attention and procedural learning.
table.randomization: The order of the underlying sequences for the SRT task will be counterbalanced to avoid order effects (West et al., 2018).
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants include two groups of 18-35 years old native English speakers with and without dyslexia. Participants will be recruited through various avenues, including SONA and social media and will be compensated with course credit or £15 Amazon gift voucher for their time. Participants with dyslexia will be adults with a previous diagnosis of dyslexia, without comorbid diagnoses. Given the limited resources available one of two possible approaches will be adopted: a) Ideally the dyslexic group will score <85 on one or more of the literacy tasks (word reading, nonword reading or spelling); b) However, given the limited resources available and potential difficulties with recruitment, a less stringent criteria may be adopted for the dyslexic population: adults that score < 90 on one or more of the literacy tasks, to avoid losing a high number of dyslexic participants. The criteria for group assignment will be selected solely based on the reading and spelling tasks, before analysing any other data.
All participants will be native English speakers, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing, vision and motor impairments that may impede task performance. Participants with Dyslexia and TD adults will be matched for age and non-verbal IQ.
Participants' scores on literacy measures will be assessed after the first session to determine whether they meet the criteria for both groups; if the criteria is not met, participants will not be asked to complete the follow-up sessions.
This study was ethically approved by the Department of Psychology Ethics Committee, University of York.
table.sample_size: The intended sample size will be 42 participants (acceptable range 42 – 50) per group who completed all sessions. Each participant will be exposed to three distinct sequences to allow sequence counterbalancing.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size was determined based on a power analysis using the test-retest reliability for the no-ISI group in our previous study (r = .42).
table.stopping_rule: Acceptable range of 42 – 50 participants per group who completed all sessions.
table.manipulated_variables:
Time of testing: three separate sessions all administered one week apart.
Group: Age-matched TD controls and adults with dyslexia
table.statistical_tests:
1. Response times and procedural learning
In order to analyse response times in the SRT task a linear mixed effects model (model 1) will be fitted with Probability (Probable vs Improbable), Epoch (successive contrasts), Session and Group (Control vs Dyslexic) as fixed effects and Participants as random effects. For the three-level factor of session two orthogonal contrasts were set: lag1 which contrasts session 1 with sessions 2 and 3 (S1 vs S2 & S3) and lag2 contrasts the performance in sessions 2 and 3.
For both response times and accuracy, all interactions between the predictors will be analysed. Following Barr et al. (2013), a backward selection from the maximal random-effects structure will be applied. The random-effects structure will be simplified according to the goodness of fit (AIC - Akaike Information Criterion; Akaike, 1974) with a smaller value indicating a better fit. When dealing with convergence issues, the random effects structure will be progressively simplified until convergence is reached (Barr et al., 2013).
Multiple comparisons will be controlled for using the Holm-Bonferroni method for the main-effects and interactions of interest. DFbetas will be calculated and standardised after model selection via the influence.ME package (Nieuwenhuis, Pelzer, & te Grotenhuis, 2012). Participants with z-scores greater than +/- 3.29 will be reported as influential cases.

To determine whether participants show evidence of procedural learning probability will be the main effect of relevance as it indicates whether there were significant differences in response times for probable and improbable trials. Additionally, the interactions between probability*epoch, probability*session and probability*epoch*session will give information about the effects of practice on procedural learning.
By analysing the main effect group and the interactions between probability*group (Age-matched controls vs Dyslexics), probability*epoch*group and probability*epoch*session*group, we will be able to determine whether there are significant differences between groups in the magnitude and trajectory of procedural learning acquisition.

Additional models will be computed to explore attention and language-related changes in procedural learning. Model 2 will include probability*session*attention*group as predictors and its interactions. This model will only be estimated on the last 600 trials. The dependent variable and random effects will remain the same. The attention measure used will depend on whether the three measures on the PVT correlate highly with the Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scales results, if so a composite measure of both tasks will be used. If not, only the PVT measures will be used as the attention index. Since the median, on the PVT, is a continuous predictor, this variable will be standardised and centered. The median will be adopted for the modelling as this variable was identified in study 3 as the most reliable measure of sustained attention in the PVT.
To determine whether there are attention-related differences in response times and procedural learning, we will analyse attention as a main effect and the interaction between attention*probability and between probability*session*attention will also provide valuable information regarding the acquisition of procedural learning as a function of attention. Of particular interest will be the interaction between probability*attention*group and probability*session*attention*group, which will allow us to determine whether there are attentional dependent differences between groups on procedural learning.
Model 3 will follow the same structure of model 2 with the variable language instead of attention. Composite measures for language will be derived for largely correlated measures (r > .5). These will also be centre and standardised. If there’s an indication of a possible interaction between attention and language measures, a fourth model including Probability*Group*Attention*Language will be fitted.

2. Data analysis - reliability

2.1 SRT task
For split-half and test-retest reliability analysis, sequence learning will be computed in two distinct manners in order to determine which measure produces more stable outcomes. Difference scores, the most commonly used procedural learning measure for the SRT task, will be computed as the simple difference between improbable and probable RTs, with a positive value indicating sequence learning; regressions slopes for each participant/session will be obtained by running a linear mixed effects model with response time as a dependent variable and probability as a predictor, for the random structure participants will be introduced as a random intercept and probability as a slope.

Split-half reliability: To measure the split-half reliability for both sessions/groups, trials will be separated into probable and improbable trials. Consecutive trials will be labelled as odd or even. The split-half reliability will be calculated by running Pearson’s correlations for procedural learning (difference scores/regression slopes) for even and odd trials.
Test-retest reliability: To measure the test-retest reliability of the SRT task, a procedural learning score will be computed for each session/group. The test-retest reliability score results from Pearson’s correlations of the procedural learning scores (difference scores/regression slopes) from session 1 and session 2 and from session 2 and 3. Bland-Altman plots will be plotted to assess the levels of agreement.
Fisher-z transformations will be performed for the split-half to verify if there is a significant difference between the split-half reliability of each group for each session. The same procedure will be used for the comparison of the test-retest reliability between groups.

2.2. PVT task

For the PVT task, some of the most used measures will be computed: lapses (number of response times equal or above 500 ms), mean RT, mean reciprocal response time (mean 1/RT) and median RT (Basner & Dinges, 2011) for each group. Additionally, an ex-gaussian analysis was performed on the PVT for each participant to determine the levels of variability of the response times distribution, i.e. the tau parameter, whose reliability was also analysed. Test-retest reliability will be computed as a Pearson correlation for each attention measure for session 1 and 2 and for session 2 and 3.

3. Relationship between language, literacy and cognitive measures and procedural learning
The relationship between nonverbal intelligence and procedural learning will be analysed first and, if the correlation between nonverbal intelligence and procedural learning is not negligible (i.e. r < .10), partial correlations controlling for nonverbal intelligence will be run for language, literacy and cognitive abilities.
Pearson correlations between language, literacy and cognitive measures and procedural learning for each session by group. The PVT measure with the highest reliability will be used in this analysis. To determine whether there are differences between groups in the size of the relationship Fisher-z transformations will be used to compare the coefficients.
An ex-gaussian analysis will also be performed on the PVT for each participant to determine whether there are differences between groups on the levels of variability of the response times distribution, i.e. the tau parameter, as this has been found to be a sensitive marker of ADHD (Gooch et al., 2012) a disorder with high comorbidity with dyslexia. The relationship between the tau parameter and language and literacy measures will also be explored.

4. Explicit awareness
Explicit awareness performance will be analysed by comparing the performance of each group in the generation task. A one-way anova will be conducted to determine whether there are significant differences between groups in the number of triplets recalled of the sequence at time 2. Analyses of the relationship between explicit awareness (number of triplets recalled) and procedural learning (difference scores) will be computed by correlating the explicit awareness measures and the difference scores.
table.transformations: Response times will be log transformed as these tend to follow a Wald distribution: rightly skewed and long tails (Brysbaert, & Stevens, 2018). By transforming the response times’ data, the residuals will then be inspected to determine whether they are normally distributed. Box Cox transformations (Box & Cox, 1964) or a generalised mixed effects model with a gamma distribution may be adopted if the residuals are not normally distributed after the log transformation.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<.05 criteria for determining which independent variables are significant predictors of the dependent variables computed by package lmerTest (Kuznetsova, Brockhoff & Christensen, 2017) for linear models, which will be adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni method (Holm, 1979) when applicable.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants with Dyslexia with comorbid diagnosis or performance within the normal range in reading and spelling tasks (i. e. > 85 or > 90, depending on the criteria for group allocation) will be excluded from the study. Similarly TD participants underperforming in the literacy tasks (i. e. < 85 or <90, depending on the criteria used for the dyslexic group) will also be excluded.
Following the procedures applied by West et al. (2018), the first two trials of each block will be removed as these are not predictable since the sequence follows a higher order structure. For all attempts at the SRT task, incorrect trials, outlier trials and trials > 5000ms will be removed from the analyses. Due to the unequal number of probable and improbable trials, a moving criterion based on sample size will be used to identify outlier response times (Selst & Jolicoeur, 1994; Cousineau & Chartier, 2010).
Participants’ performance will also be analysed based on group performance on each session. Participants whose accuracy levels and response times are 2.5 SD above or below the group mean will be excluded from the analyses. RT data will only be analysed after excluding participants with average accuracy 2.5 SD below the mean.
table.missing_data_handling: If data is missing for some tasks, the participant will still be included in the analyses of the remaining tasks.

The present task is a nonverbal probabilistic task that follows the outline described by West et al. (2018). Each task comprises two second order conditional 12 item sequences. The first two sequences were taken from Shanks, Wilkinson and Channon (2003): probable sequence A – 314324213412; improbable sequence B – 431241321423, the second sequences were taken from Schwaneveldt and Gomez (1998): probable sequence C – 121342314324; improbable sequence D – 123413214243.
For each SRT task, each block starts with the consecutive generation of two random digits (for example: 43), that bigram will then be followed by the location in sequence A (ex. 2) with 90% of probability (probable trial) or the position in sequence B (ex. 1) with 10% chance of occurrence (improbable trial). After each response a new bigram is created which will continuously follow the same principles, with no interstimulus interval.
Response times and accuracy will be measured for each trial. Participants will have to provide a response for each trial to initiate the next trial, regardless of accuracy. Responses will be scored 1 or 0 depending on whether participants press the correct key. Response times below 200 ms will be removed from the analyses and outliers will be identified based on a moving criteria (Van Selst & Jolicoeur, 1994) to replicate the procedures adopted by West et al. (2018).

Language and cognitive tasks
Language and cognitive abilities will also be measured and scored according to standardised guidelines to explore the relationship between procedural learning and individual skills as predicted by the Declarative/Procedural model (Ullman & Pierpoint, 2015). This model proposes that the declarative and procedural memory systems support different components of language, with the procedural memory system underlies the learning and processing of rule or pattern based language components, such as syntax, morphology, and phonology. Furthermore, a few specific tasks were included as they have been found to be impaired in individuals with dyslexia (e.g. nonword repetition). Thus, the following standardised tests and questionnaires were selected to ensure their adequacy for the populations included in the present study.
Adult Reading Questionnaire - a self-report screening tool designed to assess the risk of dyslexia in adults;
Expressive Vocabulary - Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence - Second Edition (WASI-II)
Reading and Spelling - Wechsler Individual Achievement Test, third edition UK (WIAT-III UK);
Nonword repetition - Comprehensive Test of Phonological Processing - Second Edition (CTOPP-2);
Sentence recall - Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals - Fifth Edition (CELF-5 UK);
Nonverbal intelligence will be measured using the Reasoning Matrix II - Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence - II (WASI- II);

Test-retest reliability: To measure the test-retest reliability of the SRT task, a procedural learning score will be computed for each session/group. The test-retest reliability score results from Pearson’s correlations of the procedural learning scores (difference scores/regression slopes) from session 1 and session 2 and from session 2 and 3. Bland-Altman plots will be plotted to assess the levels of agreement.
Fisher-z transformations will be performed for the split-half to verify if there is a significant difference between the split-half reliability of each group for each session. The same procedure will be used for the comparison of the test-retest reliability between groups.

2.2. PVT task

For the PVT task, some of the most used measures will be computed: lapses (number of response times equal or above 500 ms), mean RT, mean reciprocal response time (mean 1/RT) and median RT (Basner & Dinges, 2011) for each group. Additionally, an ex-gaussian analysis was performed on the PVT for each participant to determine the levels of variability of the response times distribution, i.e. the tau parameter, whose reliability was also analysed. Test-retest reliability will be computed as a Pearson correlation for each attention measure for session 1 and 2 and for session 2 and 3.

3. Relationship between language, literacy and cognitive measures and procedural learning
The relationship between nonverbal intelligence and procedural learning will be analysed first and, if the correlation between nonverbal intelligence and procedural learning is not negligible (i.e. r < .10), partial correlations controlling for nonverbal intelligence will be run for language, literacy and cognitive abilities.
Pearson correlations between language, literacy and cognitive measures and procedural learning for each session by group. The PVT measure with the highest reliability will be used in this analysis. To determine whether there are differences between groups in the size of the relationship Fisher-z transformations will be used to compare the coefficients.
An ex-gaussian analysis will also be performed on the PVT for each participant to determine whether there are differences between groups on the levels of variability of the response times distribution, i.e. the tau parameter, as this has been found to be a sensitive marker of ADHD (Gooch et al., 2012) a disorder with high comorbidity with dyslexia. The relationship between the tau parameter and language and literacy measures will also be explored.

4. Explicit awareness
Explicit awareness performance will be analysed by comparing the performance of each group in the generation task. A one-way anova will be conducted to determine whether there are significant differences between groups in the number of triplets recalled of the sequence at time 2. Analyses of the relationship between explicit awareness (number of triplets recalled) and procedural learning (difference scores) will be computed by correlating the explicit awareness measures and the difference scores.", "Response times will be log transformed as these tend to follow a Wald distribution: rightly skewed and long tails (Brysbaert, & Stevens, 2018). By transforming the response times’ data, the residuals will then be inspected to determine whether they are normally distributed. Box Cox transformations (Box & Cox, 1964) or a generalised mixed effects model with a gamma distribution may be adopted if the residuals are not normally distributed after the log transformation.", "We will use the standard p<.05 criteria for determining which independent variables are significant predictors of the dependent variables computed by package lmerTest (Kuznetsova, Brockhoff & Christensen, 2017) for linear models, which will be adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni method (Holm, 1979) when applicable.", "Participants with Dyslexia with comorbid diagnosis or performance within the normal range in reading and spelling tasks (i. e. > 85 or > 90, depending on the criteria for group allocation) will be excluded from the study. Similarly TD participants underperforming in the literacy tasks (i. e. < 85 or <90, depending on the criteria used for the dyslexic group) will also be excluded.
Following the procedures applied by West et al. (2018), the first two trials of each block will be removed as these are not predictable since the sequence follows a higher order structure. For all attempts at the SRT task, incorrect trials, outlier trials and trials > 5000ms will be removed from the analyses. Due to the unequal number of probable and improbable trials, a moving criterion based on sample size will be used to identify outlier response times (Selst & Jolicoeur, 1994; Cousineau & Chartier, 2010).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > .05", "p > .05", "p > .05", 
"p < .05", "ps > .05", "ps > .05", "p < .440"), Text = c("Whilst for the TD group there was a numerical improvement in test-retest reliability for later sessions, the reverse pattern was observed for the group with dyslexia (p > .05).", 
"Similar patterns were observed for both difference scores and random slopes, and there was no difference between computing procedural learning based on all 1000 trials versus the last 600 trials (p > .05).", 
"A two-way MANOVA revealed no significant differences between groups on the performance on the Psychomotor Vigilance task, for the tau parameter and median for all sessions (p > .05), thus suggesting that these groups showed comparable attentional abilities.", 
"There was no evidence of an association between procedural learning and attention abilities as measured by the Conners scale (p < .05) for both groups.", 
"There were no significant correlations between explicit awareness and procedural learning for the dyslexic group (ps > .05).", 
"There were no such correlations for the Dyslexic group (ps > .05).", 
"For both groups, recall of triplets was above chance in the inclusion condition (TD: t(40) = 7.21, p <.001; DD: t(41) = 6.12,p < .001), but not in the exclusion condition (TD: t(40) = -.78, p < .440; DD: t(42) = .43,p = .669)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .05", "p > .05", "p > .05", "ps > .05", "ps > .05", "p < .440", "p = .669", "p = .849", "p = .190"), Sentence = c("Whilst for the TD group there was a numerical improvement in test-retest reliability for later sessions, the reverse pattern was observed for the group with dyslexia (p > .05).", "Similar patterns were observed for both difference scores and random slopes, and there was no difference between computing procedural learning based on all 1000 trials versus the last 600 trials (p > .05).", "A two-way MANOVA revealed no significant differences between groups on the performance on the Psychomotor Vigilance task, for the tau parameter and median for all sessions (p > .05), thus suggesting that these groups showed comparable attentional abilities.", "There were no significant correlations between explicit awareness and procedural learning for the dyslexic group (ps > .05).", "There were no such correlations for the Dyslexic group (ps > .05).", "For both groups, recall of triplets was above chance in the inclusion condition (TD: t(40) = 7.21, p <.001; Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants are asked to respond to the position of the stimulus as quickly as possible by pressing a corresponding key on the keyboard.

Additionally, (Lum et al., 2013) observed that the size of the difference between groups diminished with age when participants had more practice on the SRTT or when they were tested on a SRTT with a second order conditional sequence (i.e. higher order sequences involve the determination of which stimulus (n) will follow is based on element n-2).
Participants are expected to demonstrate evidence of procedural learning in all sessions.
All participants were native English speakers, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision.

Participants were recruited through various avenues, including Prolific, the participant panel at the Department of Psychology, University of York, and social media, and were compensated with £15 or a £15 Amazon gift voucher for their time.
Participants were presented with an array of four rectangles displayed horizontally, with a stimulus (smiley face) appearing in one of the four positions on each trial.
Participants are asked to press the corresponding key on the keyboard to the position of the stimulus on screen as soon as possible.

The SRTT comprised two second order conditional 12 items sequences for each session, the pairs of sequences were randomised across participants, resulting in six groups, and were taken from (Shanks et al., 2003) httpshttpshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qlieGv//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?h0TIsi//www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wmpWEe probable sequence A -314324213412; improbable sequence B -431241321423; (Schvaneveldt & Gomez, 1998) : probable sequence C -121342314324; improbable sequence D -123413214243; and (Kaufman et al., 2010) : probable sequence E -121432413423; improbable sequence F -323412431421.

The first generation task, under inclusion conditions, required each participant to generate 100 guesses of the sequence learned in the SRT task in the last session; whilst in the exclusion condition participants were asked to produce a sequence as different as possible from the training sequence.

Following the generation tasks, the attention abilities of the participants were assessed using a self-report questionnaire -Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS) whilst nonverbal intelligence was assessed through the Reasoning Matrix task from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence -II (WASI-II).

Random slopes for each participant/session were obtained by running a linear mixed effects model with response time as a dependent variable and probability and group as predictors, for the random structure participants were introduced as a random intercept and probability as a slope.

Data from 17 participants (dyslexia: N = 7; TD: N = 10) was removed from the analyses as these did not meet inclusion criteria (i.e. dyslexic participants performing above the 90 percentile on at least one of the literacy measures and controls performing below the 90th percentile on literacy measures).
Since in the exclusion condition, unlike the inclusion condition, participants are asked to not generate the underlying sequence, this suggests some evidence of control over the explicit knowledge.
This is especially relevant when participants are being tested in a naturalistic setting where distractors are more likely to occur.

Secondly, if dyslexic participants are indeed able to fully compensate for their procedural learning deficits on the SRTT, it is unclear why the dyslexic group included in this study has not been able to compensate as well with the declarative system for their literacy and phonological abilities.

text.text: An impairment in the procedural memory system, responsible for the extraction and assimilation of regularities from sensory input, has been suggested to play a causal role in neurodevelopmental disorders such as dyslexia.
In this study, we compared the performance of adults with and without dyslexia on the Serial Reaction Time task across three sessions.
Alongside it, this experiment presents the first examination of the stability of procedural learning in a dyslexic population.
Across sessions, there was no evidence of an impairment in the dyslexic groups, thus lending no support to the procedural deficit hypothesis.

There was limited evidence for a relationship between language/literacy abilities and procedural learning, with only a significant association between nonword repetition and procedural learning for the dyslexic group (r = .31).
However, given that the reliability of the SRTT was well-below adequate psychometric standards in both groups, the lack of correlations between these measures may reflect attenuation.

Nonetheless, a positive correlation between attention and procedural learning was observed in both groups, suggesting that individuals with better attentional abilities showed more evidence of procedural learning in the SRTT (rs between -.34 to -.47).
In light of these findings, it is unclear whether a procedural learning impairment can account for the behavioural and cognitive profile observed in individuals with dyslexia.

The ability to extract patterns from sensory input across time and space is thought to underlie the development and acquisition of language and literacy skills (Batterink et al., 2019; Saffran, 2018; Ullman et al., 2020).

text.text: For instance, procedural learning is a core neurocognitive system implicated in the acquisition, consolidation and automatization of cognitive and motor skills and habits (Squire, 1984 (Squire, , 1994;; Squire & Zola, 1996).

Snowling et al., 2020) , is at least partly caused by a neural abnormality in this memory system (Ullman et al., 2020).

text.text: Inconsistent evidence has also been observed when examining the correlations between literacy and procedural memory (Hamrick et al., 2018; Lammertink, Boersma, Rispens, et al., 2020; Oliveira et al., 2021; Oliveira, Henderson, et al., 2023).

text.text: Whilst the absence of an association between procedural learning and literacy abilities may indicate that these constructs are unrelated, the poor psychometric properties of the tasks used to measure procedural learning may have contributed to the attenuation of the correlations between these variables (Kalra et al., 2019; Oliveira et al., 2024; Oliveira, Hayiou-Thomas, et al., 2023; Siegelman & Frost, 2015; Stark-Inbar et al., 2017; West et al., 2018).

text.text: Indeed, in order to adequately test the predictions of the Procedural Deficit Hypothesis, reliable indices of procedural memory are required.

The psychometric properties of these tasks have recently begun to be examined in typically developing populations, but to the best of our knowledge, no studies have yet investigated the stability of the procedural learning effect in disordered populations.

In our previous work with a general population sample (Oliveira et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qkgKL0 2024) , we found suggestive evidence that procedural learning effects may stabilise after multiple sessions, in line with the suggestion by (Conway et al., 2019; Palmer et al., 2018).

text.text: Here, we extend existing evidence on the psychometric properties of the Serial Reaction Time task (SRTT; (Nissen & Bullemer, 1987) , focusing on the test-retest reliability of this task across multiple sessions in populations of adults with and without dyslexia.
text.formatted: Here, we extend existing evidence on the psychometric properties of the Serial Reaction Time task (SRTT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Nissen & Bullemer, 1987)</ref> , focusing on the test-retest reliability of this task across multiple sessions in populations of adults with and without dyslexia.

text.text: With the aim of testing the PDH, we examine both group differences in procedural learning and associations between SRTT performance and measures of language and literacy and how these results manifested over different sessions of procedural learning.

Finally, we explore a putative link between procedural learning and attention in individuals with and without dyslexia as an effort to better understand the locus of procedural learning differences in dyslexia, and whether this is linked to the stability of the task in dyslexia and TD development.
The procedural/declarative model (Ullman, 2016) is one of the models that aims to explain the role of procedural memory in language acquisition.
text.formatted: The procedural/declarative model <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Ullman, 2016)</ref> is one of the models that aims to explain the role of procedural memory in language acquisition.

text.text: This model claims that the declarative memory system is responsible for the fast acquisition of arbitrary information such as lexical knowledge, whilst the procedural memory system is involved in the more gradual acquisition of probabilistic information (including phonology, grammar, reading and spelling abilities).

Focusing on literacy more specifically, children may implicitly learn and automatize the mapping between grapheme and phoneme in spelling (Gingras & Sénéchal, 2019; Treiman & Kessler, 2011) and reading (Steacy et al., 2019; Treiman, Kessler, & Bick, 2003; Treiman, Kessler, Zevin, Bick, & Davis, 2006) using statistical information in the input.

text.text: Evidence for the role of procedural memory in language learning is multifaceted.

Firstly, procedural memory and language share brain systems such as basal ganglia and frontal cortex, such that abnormalities in the procedural memory system are expected to lead to linguistic impairments (Ullman & Pierpont, 2005).

text.text: Based on this evidence, Ullman and colleagues (Ullman, 2014; Ullman et al., 2020) proposed the Procedural Deficit Hypothesis, arguing that an impairment to the procedural memory system could underlie the language and/or literacy impairments that characterise dyslexia.

text.text: Dyslexia is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder, in which the defining difficulties with word-level reading and spelling are often accompanied by an array of secondary impairments in working memory (e.g.

Fostick & Revah, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13803395.2020.1870101#), motor functioning (Ramus, Pidgeon, & Frith, 2003), executive function and attentional control (e.g. Romani et al., 2011).

text.text: The dominant theoretical account of dyslexia -the phonological deficit hypothesis -proposes a core deficit in the representation, storage and/or retrieval of speech sounds (Ramus, 2003).

text.text: The Procedural Deficit Hypothesis attempts to address this gap, suggesting that the location, severity and extent of the neuroanatomical abnormalities in the procedural memory system gives rise to multiple profiles, substantial heterogeneity across individuals with dyslexia and secondary difficulties that could emerge from dysfunctions in distinct areas of the procedural memory system and its circuitry.

Specifically, working memory, and other executive functions, are thought to be supported by the posterior parietal-anterior dorsal striatum (anterior caudate/putamen) -prefrontal circuitry (Draganski et al., 2008; Ullman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Specifically, working memory, and other executive functions, are thought to be supported by the posterior parietal-anterior dorsal striatum (anterior caudate/putamen) -prefrontal circuitry <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Draganski et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Ullman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: According to this hypothesis (Ullman et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?upWwyb 2020) , reading difficulties may be explained by the procedural dysfunction, possibly leading to perceptual impairments and difficulties in learning predictive associations that underlie the learning of grapheme-phoneme (and phoneme-grapheme) mappings.
text.formatted: According to this hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Ullman et al., 2020)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?upWwyb">,</ref> reading difficulties may be explained by the procedural dysfunction, possibly leading to perceptual impairments and difficulties in learning predictive associations that underlie the learning of grapheme-phoneme (and phoneme-grapheme) mappings.

text.text: Additionally, problems with speech-sound representations and learning of speech-sound categories may also occur since these skills are thought to be acquired implicitly, through gradual exposure to distributions of phonetic features.

Finally, the procedural deficit hypothesis proposes that individuals with dyslexia may be able to compensate for some, if not all, of their procedural deficits by relying on the declarative memory system, using strategies such as chunking, as well as drawing on semantic and explicit knowledge.

Supporting the Procedural Deficit Hypothesis, a meta-analysis conducted by (Lum et al., 2013) found evidence for smaller procedural learning effects on the Serial Reaction Time Task for individuals with dyslexia (N = 186, aged 7-15 years) compared to typically developing controls (N = 203, aged 7-15 years; average weighted standardised mean difference of .499, 95% CI [.204, .693]).

text.text: In the SRTT, one the of the most commonly used measures of procedural memory, four rectangles are typically displayed on screen with a stimulus (e.g. a smiley face) appearing in one of the four positions on each trial.
Participants are asked to respond to the position of the stimulus as quickly as possible by pressing a corresponding key on the keyboard.
Unbeknownst to the participants, the presentation of some of the stimuli follows a pattern.

Evidence of procedural learning in this task is taken as the difference between response times (RTs) for trials that follow the sequence and those which do not, on the assumption that if participants learn the sequence, they should be able to anticipate the position of the upcoming stimulus and respond faster.

Additionally, (Lum et al., 2013) observed that the size of the difference between groups diminished with age when participants had more practice on the SRTT or when they were tested on a SRTT with a second order conditional sequence (i.e. higher order sequences involve the determination of which stimulus (n) will follow is based on element n-2).

text.text: Crucially, these meta-analyses, and the majority of studies, have only examined group differences in a single practice session.
It is unclear whether performance in a single session is sufficient to probe the different stages of procedural learning.

Procedural learning is thought to involve an initial phase of fast acquisition after exposure (Doyon et al., 2009), followed by a second stage marked by a slower learning rate, trending towards an asymptote which is thought to be required for consolidation to occur (Hauptmann & Karni, 2002; Hauptmann et al., 2005; Karni et al., 1998).

text.text: As the initial memory becomes increasingly robust and resistant to interference through memory consolidation (Hauptmann et al., 2005; Nemeth et al., 2010; Song, 2009; Song, Howard, & Howard, 2007), automatisation of the new learned skill may allow for its effortless performanceoften referred to as 'proceduralisation' (Doyon & Benali, 2005).

text.text: Whilst these studies have often used the same sequences in the first and follow-up sessions, our previous findings (Oliveira et al., 2024) suggest that this may not be a requirement for consolidation and automatisation to occur as we observed a positive relationship between similarity between sequences used at test and retest and the procedural learning effect.

text.text: Thus, suggesting that some knowledge is carried on from session to session, however, with this design, the distinct stages of procedural learning cannot be isolated.

Despite this disadvantage, from a practical perspective, the adoption of distinct sequences with shared elements arguably more likely represents the input children would receive in a naturalistic environment.

Given that the earlier phase of fast acquisition may lead to substantial changes in the ranking order between test and retest due to individual differences in the learning trajectory, it is likely that once participants' gains start showing less practice effects in the procedural learning effect in later sessions that this will translate into better reliability.

It is then that the associations between measures of procedural learning and language or literacy should be most clearly apparent nor only because attenuation would occur to a lesser degree but also because this stage would likely reflect more closely the individuals' true learning ability.

text.text: A small number of studies have examined the issue of the time course of procedural learning in participants with and without dyslexia.

text.text: Due to the limited number of studies examining later sessions, we can only speculate that these differences may reflect developmental changes.

In line with (Lum et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LbJ905 2013; West, Melby-Lervåg, et al., 2021) , who reported larger group differences for children than adults, it is possible that this age difference would also be observed in later sessions, whereby adults are better able to compensate for their difficulties than children for whom the declarative memory system is still under maturation (Finn et al., 2016).

text.text: While the procedural deficit hypothesis makes clear predictions of a group-level deficit in measures of procedural learning in populations with dyslexia and other language-learning disorders, the model's predictions are more complex when taking an individual differences perspective.
This is because of the proposed compensatory role of declarative memory.
Specifically, the procedural/declarative model (Lum et al., 2012) expects procedural memory to correlate with language and literacy in typically developing populations.
text.formatted: Specifically, the procedural/declarative model <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Lum et al., 2012)</ref> expects procedural memory to correlate with language and literacy in typically developing populations.

text.text: However, if the procedural memory is impaired in dyslexia (and not supporting language/literacy abilities to the same extent) then a null correlation between procedural learning and language/literacy may be predicted.
Instead, stronger associations might be predicted between the compensatory declarative memory system and language/literacy abilities.

text.text: Nor was there any evidence that the magnitude of the association differed between TD and dyslexic groups.

However, disattenuated correlations (i.e., adjusted for reliability) revealed a large correlation between procedural learning and spelling (r = .53) for the dyslexic group, with only negligible to small correlations between language/literacy and procedural learning for the TD group.
Reconciling these contradictory findings under the procedural deficit hypothesis is difficult.

One factor that may help to account for the mixed findings in this field is the psychometric properties of the procedural learning effect that is measured by the SRTT, particularly its test-retest reliably.

Similar to other well-established paradigms within cognitive psychology (Hedge et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wgfypI 2018) , the SRTT yields robust and replicable results at the group level, but recent investigations demonstrate that it has suboptimal psychometric properties, which make it difficult to apply to individual differences research (Oliveira, Hayiou-Thomas, et al., 2023; Siegelman & Frost, 2015; West et al., 2018).

text.text: However, the role of attention in procedural learning is still under debate.

There is evidence suggesting that attention is a mechanism whichhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Jh3Kre through top-down (i.e., goal-driven) and bottom-up (i.e., stimulus-driven) processes (Awh et al., 2012; Failing & Theeuwes, 2018) , reduces the available information by selecting the relevant stimuli and allowing for the detection and extraction of regularities from the sensory input (van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019; Zhao & Luo, 2017).

text.text: Thus, it is possible that attention may be required for establishing associations between temporally separated events, particularly when learning more complex sequences (Cohen et al., 1990; Jimenez & Mendez, 1999).

text.text: Thus, whilst procedural learning is often being characterised as an automatic process independent of attentional resources, this assertion may be stage dependent: in a neuroimaging study (Thomas et al., 2004) lower activation in the parietal cortex, associated with visual-attentional processes, was observed for sequenced than random blocks in adult participants performing a deterministic SRTT.

text.text: This finding was taken to indicate that as learning becomes automatised, it becomes less dependent on visual attention.

text.text: Even though P1 and N1 are both thought to capture attention processes, evidence suggests that P1 is modulated by attentional processes related to visuospatial processing whilst N1 is modulated by evaluation of a visual target (Vogel & Luck, 2000; Warbrick et al., 2014).

text.text: When performing the SRTT, the amplitude of the P1 component decreased across sequenced trials followed by an increase in the random block, thus mirroring the procedural learning effect.
No such pattern was observed in other components such as N1 and P3, thus suggesting a decrease in the reliance on visuospatial processing over time.

To conclude, since attention may be involved in the early stages of procedural learning, it is possible that the weaknesses in attention often observed in populations with dyslexia (Ebert & Kohnert, 2011; Paulesu et al., 2014) might not only contribute to the group differences in procedural learning, but also to poorer stability of the SRTT in disordered populations as fluctuations in attention throughout the task and from day to day might contribute to changes in the procedural learning effect.

text.text: Rationale for the current study Given the recognition that adequate psychometric properties are a requirement for reliable, and potentially replicable, results (Matheson, 2019), our previous efforts have been aimed towards establishing the test-retest reliability of the probabilistic SRTT in typically developing adult samples and to investigate which factors may affect its stability.

In (Oliveira et al., 2024) we observed that increasing the number of sessions led to numerically higher stability in the SRTT (session 1-2: r = .43; session 2-3: r = .60), especially when using random slopes as opposed to simple difference scores.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Oliveira et al., 2024)</ref> we observed that increasing the number of sessions led to numerically higher stability in the SRTT (session 1-2: r = .43; session 2-3: r = .60), especially when using random slopes as opposed to simple difference scores.

text.text: The reliability for later sessions may point to the superior stability of later stages of procedural memory, however given the use of different sequences at each time point, it is likely that even at follow-up sessions earlier stages were still being captured.
Finally, when testing the assumptions of the procedural deficit hypothesis (Ullman, 2004), i.e. that language and literacy skills would correlate with procedural learning, no support was found.

text.text: Procedural learning was only found to moderately correlate with vocabulary in the third, and last, session, but not with measures of literacy, nonword repetition or sentence repetition.

Attention, on the other hand, showed a moderate relationship with procedural learning, with individuals with better offline attentional abilities showing more evidence of procedural learning in the SRTT, this is consistent with previous findings (Sengottuvel & Rao, 2013; West, Shanks, et al., 2021).

text.text: It is also possible that poor attention may increase the variability in performance throughout the task, contributing to increased noise in the procedural learning effect, and thus reduced stability.
Thus, the current study aims to determine whether attention (measured via a Psychomotor Vigilance task) is associated with both procedural learning performance and reliability.

In summary, this study examined the cognitive and procedural learning abilities of adults with dyslexia, with the aim of testing the predictions of the PDH by examining group and individual differences in procedural learning and its role in language and literacy.
Importantly, these group and individual differences were considered in the context of also examining the stability of performance on the probabilistic SRTT over three sessions.

Even though we have adopted different sequences at each time point, these were highly similar sequences, therefore at least some degree of procedural knowledge will be carried across sessions as suggested by our previous findings where similarity positively correlated with procedural learning in session 2 (Oliveira et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Even though we have adopted different sequences at each time point, these were highly similar sequences, therefore at least some degree of procedural knowledge will be carried across sessions as suggested by our previous findings where similarity positively correlated with procedural learning in session 2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Oliveira et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it is likely that this experiment will capture both earlier and later stages of procedural learning in the follow-up sessions, however it will not be possible to disentangle learning from later stages as these will likely co-occur.

We suggest that the greater stability expected in later sessions will result in more robust associations with measures of language and literacy, and provide a more sensitive test of the predictions of the procedural deficit hypothesis.
Furthermore, we aim to investigate the association between procedural learning and attention that has previously been reported in the general population.

Given the substantial variability in sustained attention observed in dyslexia, we expect that the association with the SRTT will be particularly marked in the current study, yet if the poorer attentional abilities of this group lead to a less reliable procedural learning effect, then it could result in more attenuation of the associations between these measures.
Are there group differences in procedural learning?
a.
Participants are expected to demonstrate evidence of procedural learning in all sessions.
This will be indicated by faster and more accurate responses to probable versus improbable trials, particularly during later epochs; b.
According to the procedural deficit hypothesis, adults with dyslexia are expected to show less evidence of procedural learning than TD adults; c.
Participants with dyslexia will show slower RTs than the TD group but this will not account for the differences in procedural learning when participants' average speed is taken into account; 2.
Is the procedural learning effect stable across sessions?
a.
Both groups will show higher split-half reliability than test-retest reliability, and for the control group these will be in a similar range to that found in previous studies; b.
Reliability in the dyslexic group will be either equivalent to, or lower than, that of the control group (exploratory hypothesis). c.
Higher test-retest reliability is expected for both groups for later sessions (2 and 3) than between session 1 and 2); 3.
Does procedural learning correlate with languages and literacy measures?
a.
According to the procedural/declarative model, procedural learning should correlate with language and literacy measures.
Later (more stable) sessions should in principle be more highly correlated with language/literacy, if there is a true correlation between these measures is present: i.
Empirically, given our previous findings (Oliveira submitted), these correlations are absent in TD groups; ii.
However these correlations may emerge in dyslexic participants if they exist only at the lower end; 4.
Does procedural learning correlate with offline attention measures?
a.
Both groups will demonstrate a positive correlation between procedural learning and sustained attention, as measured by the PVT task; b.
Adults with dyslexia are expected to show higher intra-individual variability in sustained attention than TD adults; c.
Participants with higher intra-individual variability in sustained attention will show lower test-retest reliability in the SRT task; 5.
Do participants with and without dyslexia differ in the amount of explicit awareness of the sequence?
a.

text.text: All participants were native English speakers, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision.

Adults with dyslexia confirmed having received a formal diagnosis of dyslexia and not having other documented neurodevelopmental disorders.

text.text: The experiment used a mixed-subjects design with each participant performing the SRTT at three time points approximately one week apart.
All sessions started with the administration of the SRTT followed by the standardised tests in all sessions.
The nonverbal probabilistic Serial Reaction Time task used in the present study follows the protocol outlined in (Oliveira et al., 2024).

text.text: Participants were presented with an array of four rectangles displayed horizontally, with a stimulus (smiley face) appearing in one of the four positions on each trial.
Participants are asked to press the corresponding key on the keyboard to the position of the stimulus on screen as soon as possible.
Trials only proceed once a response is made.

Unknown to the participant, and given the probabilistic nature of this task, the position of the stimuli on screen follows either a probable (90% of the trials) or an improbable (10% of the trials) sequence.

Procedural learning in this task is reflected in a difference in RTs between improbable and probable trials, since learning of the underlying sequence would allow participants to anticipate the position of the following stimulus.

text.text: The first generation task, under inclusion conditions, required each participant to generate 100 guesses of the sequence learned in the SRT task in the last session; whilst in the exclusion condition participants were asked to produce a sequence as different as possible from the training sequence.
Each sequence generated by the participants was coded into the total amount of triplets recalled.

Following the generation tasks, the attention abilities of the participants were assessed using a self-report questionnaire -Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS) whilst nonverbal intelligence was assessed through the Reasoning Matrix task from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence -II (WASI-II).
All cognitive measures were delivered and scored in accordance with manual instructions.

At the end of each session, sustained attention was measured experimentally through a 5-min version of the Psychomotor Vigilance task (Reifman et al., 2018) to further explore the relationship between attention and procedural learning.

text.text: RTs were grouped into epochs of 200 trials.

Note that the first two trials of each epoch were removed for the purposes of analysis, as these are not predictable in the current task structure, which uses second-order conditionals (requiring participants to consider the positions of the two previous trials to be able to predict the following position).

Outlier RTs were identified using a moving criterion based on sample size given the uneven number of probable and improbable trials, with the cutoff point depending on the number of correct trials per condition and block (Cousineau & Chartier, 2010; Van Selst & Jolicoeur, 1994).

text.text: The residuals were then inspected to determine whether they met the assumptions of normality for fitting the linear mixed effects models.
Linear mixed models were fitted to the RTs in order to compare the performance of adults with and without dyslexia.
An initial model comprised Probability (Probable vs Improbable), Epoch (successive contrasts), Session and Group (Control vs Dyslexic) as fixed effects and Participants as random effects.
For the three-level factor of session two orthogonal contrasts were set: lag1 which contrasts session 1 with sessions 2 and 3 (S1 vs S2 & S3) and lag2 contrasts the performance in sessions 2 and 3.

text.text: All dichotomous variables were contrasted using effect coding.
All interactions between the predictors were analysed.

Following theoretical evidence and Barr et al.'s (2013) recommendation, a backward selection from the maximal random-effects structure was fitted, with the random structure being simplified if necessary due to convergence issues according to the goodness of fit (AIC -Akaike Information Criterion; (Akaike, 1974)) with a smaller value indicating a better fit.

text.text: H1, H3 and H4: Assessing group differences in procedural learning and the role of language, literacy and attention on the procedural learning effect
Five additional models exploring the role of language and attention abilities on procedural memory were fitted.
All models include Probability, Session and Group as fixed effects, with the addition of a predictor for language and attention, depending on the model.

These models did not include Epoch as a fixed effect (unlike the initial model described above), and were estimated on the last 600 trials when learning is expected to be more robust, in order to avoid computational issues.
The dependent variable and random effects remained the same.
For the models including language and literacy abilities as a predictor, all measures were centred and standardised.

To establish the reliability of the SRTT, two measures of procedural learning were computed: difference scores and random slopes.

Difference scores, the most commonly used procedural learning measure for the SRTT, were computed as the simple difference between improbable and probable RTs, with a positive value indicating procedural learning.

Random slopes for each participant/session were obtained by running a linear mixed effects model with response time as a dependent variable and probability and group as predictors, for the random structure participants were introduced as a random intercept and probability as a slope.
To measure the split-half reliability for both sessions/groups, trials were separated into probable and improbable trials.
Consecutive trials were labelled as odd or even.
The split-half reliability was calculated by running Pearson's correlations for procedural learning (difference scores/random slopes) for even and odd trials.

Pearson's correlations between the procedural learning scores (difference scores/random slopes) from session 1 and session 2 and from session 2 and 3 for each group were taken as measures of test-retest reliability.
Bland-Altman plots (Bland & Altman, 1986) were plotted to assess the levels of agreement.

Furthermore, and similar to the initial model described in the previous section, these models indicate that overall RTs decreased with practice across sessions (significant effect of Session for one or both contrasts).

Most relevant for the aims of the study, and contrary to our hypothesis, there was no evidence that Literacy, Nonword repetition or Sentence repetition predicted the procedural learning effect, as evidenced by the non-significant interactions between Probability and these variables.

Similar to previous models in this study, there was clear evidence of procedural learning as evidenced by a Probability effect, which again benefitted from practice as evidenced by the two-way interaction between Probability and Session for Delay1.

The trend for an interaction between Probability x Group x Session for Delay1 indicates that the TD group showed a larger procedural learning effect than the dyslexic group from session 1 to 2, but this contrast did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

This experiment is the first to examine the procedural learning abilities of adults with and without dyslexia in the context of task reliability over 3 learning sessions.

Alongside taking a group level approach to examining differences in procedural learning, we also adopted an individual differences approach, comprehensively examining relationships between procedural learning and language, literacy and attention.

Both groups showed robust procedural learning effects and we found no support for the procedural deficit hypothesis at the group-level: There were no differences between groups in the magnitude or trajectory of the procedural learning effect within or across sessions.

Furthermore, and compatible with our previous findings, there was only very limited evidence for a relationship between procedural learning and language/literacy, with only a significant and moderate correlation between procedural learning and nonword repetition in the dyslexic group.

This could be at least partially explained by the poor psychometric properties of the SRTT, as again the procedural learning effect in the SRTT failed to meet psychometric standards in both typical and atypical populations (rs < .70).
text.formatted: This could be at least partially explained by the poor psychometric properties of the SRTT, as again the procedural learning effect in the SRTT failed to meet psychometric standards in both typical and atypical populations (rs < .70).

text.text: Numerically higher reliability in later sessions was observed in the TD group than in earlier sessions, replicating the pattern observed in our previous study.
Unexpectedly, the opposite pattern was observed for the dyslexic group.

Irrespective of the psychometric issues, we replicated the correlation between attention and procedural learning in both groups, suggesting that the relationship between attention and procedural learning is stronger, and more robust to the limitations of weak psychometric properties, than the relationship between procedural learning and language and literacy abilities.

As predictedhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MwqNtB and replicating our previous research (Oliveira et al., 2024) , we found higher split-half than test-retest reliability for procedural learning in both groups, particularly in sessions 1 and 3.
text.formatted: As predicted, and replicating our previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Oliveira et al., 2024)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MwqNtB">,</ref> we found higher split-half than test-retest reliability for procedural learning in both groups, particularly in sessions 1 and 3.

text.text: Crucially, the test-retest reliability was well below psychometric standards for both groups, indicating that the SRTT may not be suitable to be used to assess procedural learning in typical or atypical populations.

Even though the test-retest reliability improved from earlier (sessions 1-2) to later sessions (sessions 2-3) in TD participants (akin to (Oliveira et al., 2024)), the opposite pattern was observed for the dyslexic group.
text.formatted: Even though the test-retest reliability improved from earlier (sessions 1-2) to later sessions (sessions 2-3) in TD participants (akin to <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Oliveira et al., 2024)</ref>), the opposite pattern was observed for the dyslexic group.

text.text: Nonetheless, it is important to emphasise that these patterns were only numerical, and did not represent a statistically significant difference across sessions.

It is notable that the retest reliability coefficients were lower here (TD group session 1-2: rs = -.02 -.07; TD group session 2-3: rs = .33 -.34; dyslexic group session 1-2: rs = .14 -.38; dyslexic group session 2-3: rs = .00 -.11) than in our previous study (session 1-2: r = .43; session 2-3: r = .60).

Whilst it is unclear what factors account for this, these findings only further highlight the poor stability of the procedural learning effect in the SRTT, whereby designs which have yielded better reliability in the previous literature (e.g., (West, Shanks, et al., 2021)) will likely fail to produce the same findings.
text.formatted: Whilst it is unclear what factors account for this, these findings only further highlight the poor stability of the procedural learning effect in the SRTT, whereby designs which have yielded better reliability in the previous literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(West, Shanks, et al., 2021)</ref>) will likely fail to produce the same findings.

text.text: Instead, it is possible that, irrespective of the experimental design, individual differences in confounding factors may primarily contribute to the reliability of the SRTT.

Specifically, unlike in our previous study examining the psychometric properties of the SRTT in TD adults across 3 sessions, in this study individual differences in the age of the participants, their enjoyment in performing the SRTT and the degree of explicit awareness influenced the magnitude of the procedural learning effect.
Whilst enjoyment showed a positive relationship with procedural learning, explicit awareness and age showed the opposite pattern.
Thus, it is likely that the effect of these variables on procedural learning may have contributed to changes in ranking order between sessions.
The influence of these variables is not inherently problematic, as they could influence participants' performance in the same manner across sessions, thus preserving the ranking order.

However, given the poor reliability and the changes in the correlations between sessions, it is unlikely that these variables exert the same degree of influence on each session and/or their influence on each participant is consistent across sessions.
Whilst attention was not a predictor of procedural learning in the mixed model, the correlation between attention and procedural learning was replicated.

The findings from the mixed model likely reflect low power, as there was only one score per session for the attentional abilities of the participants, thus a four-way interaction was unlikely to emerge even if there was evidence for an effect of attention on procedural learning.
Future research should overcome these limitations by recruiting more participants or using online measures of attention.
Importantly, unlike our previous study with TD adults, attention correlated with procedural learning in later rather than earlier sessions.

Thus, even though attention has been suggested to be required for procedural learning to occur by reducing the sensory input to the relevant information, this correlation emerges later than the procedural learning effect.
Thus potentially highlighting the importance of top-down mechanisms whilst performing the same repetitive and long task for the third time.
This is especially relevant when participants are being tested in a naturalistic setting where distractors are more likely to occur.

Furthermore, the relationship between attention and procedural learning in the third session cannot be explained by explicit awareness, as this association remained significant after accounting for explicit awareness in the last session.

Finally, however, we cannot rule out the possibility that the timeline of the correlations between attentional abilities and procedural learning may simply reflect the poor psychometric properties of the SRTT, whereby attenuation would be more accentuated in earlier than later sessions in the TD group, and the opposite pattern for the dyslexic group.

Interestingly, despite comparable attentional abilities, the dyslexic group did not show correlations between procedural learning and attention in the last session, instead the only correlation emerged in session 2.
It is unclear whether these differences are associated with the stages of procedural learning.
Since we adopted different sequences on each session, despite their high degree of similarity, it is possible that later sessions may not represent later stages of procedural learning, per se.

Furthermore, if later sessions were to reflect later stages of procedural learning, then performance on the third session would likely be more automatised and thus less reliant on attentional resources (Seger & Spiering, 2011).
text.formatted: Furthermore, if later sessions were to reflect later stages of procedural learning, then performance on the third session would likely be more automatised and thus less reliant on attentional resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Seger & Spiering, 2011)</ref>.
